title: 26. A Great Locomotive: Amelia Flygare
book: At the Pulpit: 185 Years of Discourses by Latter-day Saint Women
notes: 61 discourses; Church Historians Press; didactic illustrations

Lucy F. Stringham, president of the South Davis Stake YLMIA, spoke after Flygare at this training meeting, focusing on the value of reliability. (“Officers’ Notes: The June Conference,”Young Woman’s Journal27, no. 7 [July 1916]: 446; see alsochapter 23herein.)
Laura P. Nicholson, “Division of Responsibility,”Young Woman’s Journal27, no. 7 (July 1916): 444.
Young Women General Board Minutes, vol. 8, 1914–1917, June 10, 1916, 55, 57, CHL; “Officers’ Notes: The June Conference,” 440–449.
SeeMatthew 25:14–30.

Just before Flygare spoke, Laura P. Nicholson, president of the Ensign Stake YLMIA, talked about the division of work: “Division of responsibility in Mutual Improvement work is one of vital importance and one upon which depends the success of any association. The work is so great that no president or presidency can carry it alone and make it a success. … Each member has a certain line of work to look after, and thus the responsibility is divided and the efficiency increased.” (Nicholson, “Division of Responsibility,” 444.)

A counselor in the YLMIA general presidency, Ruth May Fox, spoke after Flygare and used another metaphor to teach the same principle: “It is the spirit of the hive that accomplishes things. There is no seen force in the hive to direct, and yet every bee and every little community of bees knows just exactly what to do because of the spirit of the hive; and so, in our church, and in our organizations, it is the spirit that is the great moving power. It is necessary for us to understand and to put into practice all this detailed work, but we must rely upon the spirit of the work to do it successfully.” (Ruth May Fox, “Enlistment Work,”Young Woman’s Journal27, no. 7 [July 1916]: 446.)

An earlier article in a church periodical also extolled the importance of choristers: “There is probably no reason why choristers should not feel as if they had a mission; why they should not be set apart to this end; or why, when so acting, that they also are the veritable servants and handmaidens of God, and of Zion and its prophets.” (H. W. Naisbitt, “Music and Her Sister, Song,”Contributor12, no. 6 [Apr. 1891]: 237.)

Mabel M. Cooper, a member of the YLMIA general board and assistant music director, spoke earlier in the meeting about the new YLMIA songbook published by the general board. (“Officers’ Notes: The June Conference,” 441;YLMIA Song Book, Volume 1: Quartettes, Trios, Solos and Duet for Ladies’ Voices[Salt Lake City: Young Ladies’ Mutual Improvement Association, 1916].)

Fox responded to Flygare: “As Sister Flygare indicated about the girl who had done her work dutifully, and to whom we should say, ‘You have been a good girl, you have done your work well, and I am going to give you lots of work,’ so we say to you, the more you do and the better you do it, the more you will be asked to do. And this will be so even in the kingdom—the greatest reward that the Latter-day Saint expects in the kingdom of God is that the Lord will say, ‘You have been faithful over a few things, and I will make you a steward over many things.’ … The more you do and the better you do it, the more you will be asked to do here and hereafter.” (Fox, “Enlistment Work,” 447.)
Wilford Woodruff was the fourth president of the church from 1889 to 1898.
“Amelia H. Flygare Dies at Afton, Buried in Ogden,”Star Valley (WY) Independent,Aug. 26, 1948.

Flygare may be referring to the time Woodruff spent with his plural wife Sarah Elinore Brown Woodruff at their farm in Randolph, Rich County, Utah. (Thomas G. Alexander,Things in Heaven and Earth: The Life and Times of Wilford Woodruff, a Mormon Prophet[Salt Lake City: Signature Books, 1991], 135, 222–227.)

Wilford Woodruff, “Discourse Delivered at the Weber Stake Conference, Ogden, Monday, October 19th, 1896,”Deseret Weekly,Nov. 7, 1896, 641. Before becoming church president, Woodruff was named general superintendent of the Young Men’s Mutual Improvement Association at the general church conference held on April 6, 1880. (“Association Intelligence,”Contributor1, no. 8 [May 1880]: 190–192.)

YLMIA president Mattie Horne Tingey opened this meeting with a discussion about the responsibility of officers: “There is no one thing in which you need to be more careful and more particular and in which you need to seek the Lord for wisdom and guidance more than in the selection of your class leaders. … Their influence over the girls is great, and you want to be sure that they are women of good, strong character and have the love of God in their hearts, the love of Mutual Improvement work in their hearts, and a thorough love for the girls and a desire to help them.” (Martha H. Tingey, “Greeting,”Young Woman’s Journal27, no. 7 [July 1916]: 441.)
“Personal Mention,”Kindergarten Review8, no. 7 (Mar. 1898): 483; see also Amelia Flygare, 1900 U.S. Census, Ogden Ward 4, Weber Co., UT.

“Amelia H. Flygare Dies at Afton”; “The Larger Outside Cities: Ogden,”Deseret Evening News,Mar. 10, 1917; Lilliebell Falck,“Lest We Forget”: Our World War Heroes(Ogden, UT: privately printed, 1927), 43.
“Funeral Rites Set for Mrs. Flygare,”Deseret News,Aug. 24, 1948.

Flygare became the first Relief Society president of the Ogden Eighteenth Ward in 1924. (Ogden Eighteenth Ward, Mount Ogden Stake, Relief Society Minutes and Records, vol. 1, 1924–1925, Sept. 2, 1924, 11, 77, CHL.)

Flygare was appointed first counselor to Bertha M. Eccles on September 8, 1901. She was named president on October 1, 1905. She concluded that service in January 1909, after she was asked to serve as a counselor in the Weber Stake YLMIA presidency in December 1908. (Ogden Fifth Ward, Weber Stake, Young Women’s Mutual Improvement Association Minute Book, vol. 2, 1896–1904, Sept. 8, 1901, 299; Oct. 1, 1905, 41, CHL; “Officers’ Notes,”Young Woman’s Journal20, no. 4 [Apr. 1909]: 196; Ogden Fifth Ward YWMIA Minute Book, vol. 3, 1904–1909, Jan. 12, 1909, 160.)

Flygare was appointed second counselor to Aggie H. Stevens on December 23, 1908. When Stevens was replaced as stake YLMIA president by Martha B. Cooley on May 5, 1909, Flygare became first counselor. Flygare was named president on April 23, 1911, ending her service in 1922. (“Officers’ Notes,” 196; “Officers’ Notes,”Young Woman’s Journal20, no. 11 [Nov. 1909]: 571; Weber Stake Young Women’s Mutual Improvement Association Conference Minute Book, vol. 5, 1904–1918, Apr. 23, 1911, 39, CHL; “M.I.A. Notes,”Young Woman’s Journal33, no. 7 [July 1922]: 406.)
Susa Young Gates,History of the Young Ladies’ Mutual Improvement Association of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints(Salt Lake City: Deseret News, 1911), 482.
